title: "Cosine Similarity"
description: "A measure of the angle-based similarity between two nonzero vectors."
term: "Cosine Similarity"
letter: "C"

difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Cosine similarity compares the directions of two vectors. It is often
used to compare text or image embeddings, where a higher value indicates
that the vectors point in more similar directions.

## Technical explanation

For nonzero vectors $a$ and $b$, cosine similarity is
$\frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}$. It ranges from -1 to 1 in general,
though nonnegative embedding spaces often produce values in a narrower
range. Implementations need to handle zero vectors and may normalize
vectors before comparison.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Cosine similarity is used in semantic search, clustering, deduplication,
and recommendation. Its usefulness depends on the embedding model,
normalization, and application-specific evaluation; similarity alone
does not establish semantic equivalence.

## How it works

The dot product measures both direction and magnitude, so cosine
similarity divides it by the product of vector lengths:

$$
\operatorname{cosine}(a,b) =
\frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}
$$

This normalization makes the measure depend on the angle between the
vectors rather than their magnitudes.

## Practical example

A search system can embed a question and candidate document passages,
calculate cosine similarity, and rank passages by score before applying
additional relevance checks.

## Common misconceptions

- A high cosine similarity is not proof that two texts have the same
  meaning or are factually consistent.
- Cosine similarity is undefined for a zero-length vector without a
  special handling rule.
- It is not always the best metric; the embedding model and task determine
  which distance measure is appropriate.
